title: Massage techniques
metaDescription: Massage techniques in Brighton, MI: deep tissue, sports, prenatal and myofascial work, craniosacral therapy and manual lymphatic drainage.
lead: Eleven techniques, one approach: each session is built around how you feel, move and recover. Here is what each technique is, how it feels, and when it’s often chosen.

notSure.title: You don’t need to choose
notSure.body: Most sessions blend several techniques. Tell us how you feel and what you’d like to be different, and we’ll choose and adjust as we go. If you have a preference, say so when you book.

groups.title: Release deep or stubborn tension
groups.lead: Focused, firmer work for knots, overworked muscles and tension that keeps coming back.

groups.title: Free up movement
groups.lead: Slow, sustained work on the connective tissue (fascia) that wraps and links everything, for stiffness and restricted range.

groups.title: Calm, restore and recover
groups.lead: Lighter, quieter work for stress, recovery and comfort when your body needs less, not more.

techniques.name: Deep tissue massage
techniques.summary: Slower, firmer pressure that works through the surface muscles into the deeper layers of muscle and connective tissue.
techniques.feelsLike: Firm and focused, but never a contest. You set the pressure, and we check in as we go.
oftenChosenFor: Persistent tightness that lighter massage doesn’t reach
Recovery from heavy training or physically demanding work
Areas that have been tense for a long time
techniques.goodToKnow: Some muscle soreness for a day or two afterwards is common. Gentle movement and staying hydrated help.

techniques.name: Trigger point therapy
techniques.summary: Steady pressure on tight, tender spots in a muscle (trigger points) until they ease. These spots can send sensation elsewhere, like shoulder tension you feel as a tension headache.
techniques.feelsLike: Pinpoint pressure that may feel intense, then softens as the spot releases. You stay in control of how much.
oftenChosenFor: Knots you can put a finger on
Tension that seems to travel, such as from the shoulders up into the head
Tightness from desk work, driving or repetitive tasks

techniques.name: Neuromuscular therapy
techniques.summary: A methodical approach that works muscle by muscle, looking at posture, movement and tender areas together to find and ease the pattern behind recurring tension.
techniques.feelsLike: Thorough and precise: moderate to firm pressure, with more conversation about what you notice.
oftenChosenFor: Tension that keeps returning to the same places
Strain linked to posture or how you move at work
Understanding your own tension patterns, not just easing them for a day

techniques.name: Active Release Techniques
techniques.summary: Precise pressure combined with movement: we hold contact on a specific spot while you (or we) move the area through its range, to free tissue that has become stuck.
techniques.feelsLike: Active and specific. Short, focused passes rather than long strokes, and you’ll be asked to move.
oftenChosenFor: A movement that feels caught or restricted
Tightness from repetitive use in sport, trades or desk work
Getting back to an activity after a period of strain
techniques.goodToKnow: A.R.T. is a certified technique. We’ll use it where it fits your session, often alongside other work.

techniques.name: Sports massage
techniques.summary: Massage planned around your training and events: brisk and energizing before you compete, slower and deeper for recovery afterwards, and steady maintenance through a training block.
techniques.feelsLike: Purposeful and varied, from quick, light work before an event to firmer work on recovery days. Often includes stretching and movement.
oftenChosenFor: Recovery during heavy training or a race season
Preparing for, or recovering from, a race, game or event
Keeping hard-working muscles moving well between sessions
techniques.goodToKnow: Tell us your training plan and event dates. We keep work light in the day or two before an event and save deeper work for recovery days.

techniques.name: Myofascial release
techniques.summary: Slow, sustained pressure and stretching of the fascia, the connective tissue that wraps and links your muscles, to ease restrictions between layers. Often uses little or no oil, and may include skin rolling.
techniques.feelsLike: Slow and patient: a gradual stretch or melting sensation rather than kneading.
oftenChosenFor: General stiffness or feeling ‘tight all over’
Restricted range of motion
Areas around old, fully healed scars

techniques.name: Organ-specific fascial mobilization
techniques.summary: Gentle, specific pressure through the abdomen, ribs and pelvis to ease tension in the connective tissue around the organs, so the trunk can move more freely.
techniques.feelsLike: Quiet and gentle. Light, sustained hands-on contact, mostly over clothing or a drape.
oftenChosenFor: Long-standing back, neck or pelvic tension that hasn’t eased with other work
A tight or restricted feeling through the ribs, belly or pelvis
Restriction after abdominal surgery, once fully healed and cleared
techniques.goodToKnow: After surgery, or during pregnancy, we’ll talk first and may ask for clearance from your healthcare team.

techniques.name: Craniosacral therapy
techniques.summary: Very light, still holds at the head, spine and sacrum, the area at the base of the spine, to help the body settle and release tension.
techniques.feelsLike: Deeply calm. Little movement, often fully clothed, and many people drift toward sleep.
oftenChosenFor: Stress and a nervous system that feels ‘switched on’
Tension in the head, jaw and neck
When firmer massage feels like too much

techniques.name: Manual lymphatic drainage
techniques.summary: Very light, slow, rhythmic strokes that follow the direction of the lymphatic system, the network that carries fluid back toward the heart, to support healthy fluid movement.
techniques.feelsLike: Light and soothing, much lighter than people expect. It works on the skin and just below it, not the muscles.
oftenChosenFor: Swelling or puffiness after surgery, once your surgeon has cleared you
Feeling heavy or fluid-retentive, such as in late pregnancy, with clearance
Gentle recovery when your body needs less, not more
techniques.goodToKnow: Not suitable with an active infection, a blood clot or some heart and kidney conditions. After surgery, or if you have lymphedema, we’ll ask for clearance and coordinate with your healthcare team.

techniques.name: Prenatal massage
techniques.summary: Massage adapted to each stage of pregnancy, with side-lying positions and supportive cushions so you can rest comfortably and safely.
techniques.feelsLike: Supported and unhurried. Gentle to moderate pressure, adjusted as your body changes.
oftenChosenFor: Back, hip and leg discomfort as pregnancy progresses
Trouble getting comfortable or resting well
Time to slow down and feel supported, through pregnancy and the months after
techniques.goodToKnow: Let us know how far along you are and about any pregnancy complications when you book. With some, such as a high-risk pregnancy, we’ll ask for your provider’s OK first.

techniques.name: Myomassology
techniques.summary: A whole-person approach that integrates massage with reflexology, aromatherapy, craniosacral and energy-balancing work, chosen around how you feel that day.
techniques.feelsLike: Flowing and restorative, adapted as the session goes. Pressure ranges from gentle to moderate.
oftenChosenFor: Stress, and feeling depleted or out of balance
A first massage, or returning after a long break
A session built around the whole person, not one area
